sets.title: Pick-your-own strawberries
sets.passage: Come to the Pellridge farm this June and pick your own strawberries! Our fields are open every Saturday and Sunday from eight until four. We give you a basket at the gate, and you pay only for the fruit you take home. Children under six come in free with an adult. Please wear strong shoes, because the paths between the rows can be muddy after rain. Our farm shop also sells fresh jam and cold lemonade. You can find us just past the old mill on the road out of Rellbury.

sets.title: Hail in the garden
sets.passage: This morning my mother woke me at six because the weather report said there might be hail in the afternoon. We spent the whole morning putting old sheets over the lettuce and the young peppers in our garden. My arms hurt by lunch. At three o'clock the sky went dark, and white balls of ice the size of peas bounced across the yard for ten minutes. Afterwards I lifted the sheets. Every plant underneath was fine, but the beans by the fence had holes in their leaves. Next time we will need more sheets.

sets.title: The ripening gas
sets.passage:
Have you ever noticed that a bowl of fruit often seems to ripen all at once? There is a simple reason for this. As many fruits ripen, they give off a gas called ethylene. The gas is invisible, but it works like a signal. When nearby fruit takes in the gas, it begins to ripen as well, and then it releases more ethylene of its own.

Ripening brings several changes. The fruit becomes softer, and its color often changes from green to yellow or red. In bananas and many other fruits, starch turns into sugar, so the fruit tastes sweeter. Bananas, tomatoes and avocados keep ripening after they are picked. Other fruits, such as grapes, strawberries and oranges, do not ripen much more once they leave the plant.

Farmers and shops make use of these facts. Bananas are usually picked while they are still green and hard, because firm fruit travels well on long journeys. Near the end of the trip, they are often kept in warm rooms with a little added ethylene, which helps them ripen evenly before they reach the shops.

You can use the same idea at home. To ripen a hard avocado faster, put it in a paper bag with a ripe banana. The bag holds the gas close to the avocado. To slow ripening down, keep ripe fruit away from other fruit, or store it somewhere cool.

sets.title: The Rellford plank road
sets.passage:
In the spring of 1846, a farmer named Obadiah Raddle needed three days to haul a wagon of wheat to the market town of Rellford, a journey of only eighteen miles. The road was a strip of bare earth that turned to deep mud whenever it rained, and wagons regularly sank to their axles. Farmers in the valley could grow plenty of grain; the difficulty was getting it to buyers before it spoiled or before prices fell.

That autumn, a group of Rellford merchants led by Osmond Quarles formed a company to build something new to the region: a plank road. Workers laid two long timber beams along the route and nailed thick boards across them, side by side, like the floor of an enormous wooden hallway. The company planned to recover its costs through tolls. At gates every few miles, a keeper collected a small fee from each wagon before lifting the wooden bar that stretched across the road.

For the first few years, the road seemed a triumph. A team of horses could pull nearly twice its usual load over the smooth boards, and the trip from the valley to Rellford shrank from three days to a single day. Farmers paid the tolls without complaint, because the time they saved was worth far more than the fee. The company paid its owners generous profits, and newspapers in neighbouring districts urged their own towns to follow the example of Rellford.

The planks, however, were made of wood, and wood laid on damp ground decays. Within five years many boards had warped or split, and those resting directly on wet soil had begun to rot from beneath. Loose planks tipped up under passing wheels, and more than one horse broke a leg in a hole where a board had been. Repairs grew more frequent and more expensive each season, until they swallowed nearly all of the toll money.

The founders had made a careful estimate of what the road would cost to build, but they had treated that cost as something paid once. They had made no real plan for replacing every board within a decade, which is roughly how long the planks lasted. By 1857 the company's income had fallen below its repair bills, and its owners handed the road over to the county. Officials removed the remaining planks and spread a thick layer of gravel in their place.

It would be easy to remember the Rellford plank road simply as a failure, yet the story is more complicated. The road had shown valley farmers, for the first time, how much a dependable route to market was worth to them. When the county later asked them to pay a small yearly tax to keep the gravel road in good condition, they agreed by a wide margin. Having once travelled quickly, they were unwilling to go back to the mud.

items.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Boards laid on wet soil rotted from beneath and made one road dangerous for horses.
A wooden toll road did well, then failed over unplanned repairs, but still changed what farmers valued.
Good roads have played an important part in the way that farmers bring their crops to market and sell them.
A plank road was well built, but farmers refused its tolls and soon went back to using the mud.
items.correct_answer: A wooden toll road did well, then failed over unplanned repairs, but still changed what farmers valued.
items.explanation: "A wooden toll road did well, then failed over unplanned repairs, but still changed what farmers valued." is correct: the road "seemed a triumph" at first, failed because the founders "had made no real plan for replacing every board", yet the road showed farmers "how much a dependable route to market was worth to them".

distractor_rationales.choice: A plank road was well built, but farmers refused its tolls and soon went back to using the mud.
distractor_rationales.reason: "A plank road was well built, but farmers refused its tolls and soon went back to using the mud." is wrong about what happened: "Farmers paid the tolls without complaint", and in the end "they were unwilling to go back to the mud".

distractor_rationales.choice: Boards laid on wet soil rotted from beneath and made one road dangerous for horses.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Boards laid on wet soil rotted from beneath and made one road dangerous for horses." is one detail from paragraph 4 ("those resting directly on wet soil had begun to rot from beneath"); it leaves out the early success, the planning mistake and the lasting effect described in "the story is more complicated".

distractor_rationales.choice: Good roads have played an important part in the way that farmers bring their crops to market and sell them.
distractor_rationales.reason: "Good roads have played an important part in the way that farmers bring their crops to market and sell them." is too general: the passage is about one road, "the Rellford plank road", why it failed, and what it taught "valley farmers".

items.explanation: "pole" is correct: the keeper was "lifting the wooden bar that stretched across the road" to let a wagon through, so the bar is a long pole across the road.

distractor_rationales.reason: "pub" is a meaning of "bar" (a place that serves drinks), but a keeper cannot lift a building; the text says he was "lifting the wooden bar that stretched across the road".

distractor_rationales.reason: "slab" is close to a meaning of "bar" (a bar of soap or chocolate), but this bar is long and thin enough to reach over a road: "the wooden bar that stretched across the road".

distractor_rationales.reason: "ban" is close to a meaning of "bar" (something that forbids, as when a person is barred from a place), but the keeper was "lifting the wooden bar", so it is a wooden object, not a ban.

distractor_rationales.choice: The fee was lower than the cost of mending their broken wagons.
distractor_rationales.reason: "The fee was lower than the cost of mending their broken wagons." is wrong: the passage gives a different reason, "because the time they saved was worth far more than the fee", and says nothing about wagon repairs.

distractor_rationales.reason: "The county required every wagon on the road to pay it." is wrong: the tolls were the company's, which "planned to recover its costs through tolls"; the county only took the road over later, when "its owners handed the road over to the county".

distractor_rationales.reason: "They paid one small fee for a whole year of trips." is wrong: the fee was paid on every trip, since "a keeper collected a small fee from each wagon", and the reason they paid was "because the time they saved was worth far more than the fee".

distractor_rationales.reason: "to give an example of a farmer who refused to pay the tolls" is wrong: his journey was "In the spring of 1846", before the company was formed "That autumn", and later "Farmers paid the tolls without complaint".

distractor_rationales.reason: "to show how much more grain farmers grew after the road opened" is wrong: the story comes before the road existed, and the farmers already "could grow plenty of grain; the difficulty was getting it to buyers".
